newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn's Maastricht broker says EMU delay no taboo.
newsitem.headline: Bonn's Maastricht broker says EMU delay no taboo.

text.p: Germany's chief negotiator for the 1991 Maastricht treaty, the pact that set stiff guidelines for European economic and monetary union, said on Saturday that a possible delay in EMU should not be a taboo subject.

Horst Koehler, who as state secretary for finance haggled for months with Bonn's European Union partners to impose the tough convergence criteria for the euro, said a single EU currency was a desirable goal but it had to have a solid foundation based on respect for the criteria.

Der Spiegel magazine reported that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer had asked in closed-door meetings whether Germany and France should consider delaying the planned 1999 start of EMU now that both had trouble meeting the targets.

A Bundesbank spokesman said Tietmeyer had not suggested a delay in his last interview with Spiegel, which was in March. Spiegel said it had learned about Tietmeyer's reported suggestion independently through its own sources.
"The euro is, on the whole, desirable but it should start on a credible basis," Koehler, now president of the Association of German Savings and Clearing Banks, told ARD television.
If the criteria are not met, he said, "a delay cannot be taboo."

Koehler told Spiegel in March he believed watering down EMU's convergence criteria would make markets suspicious, causing foreign exchange turbulence rather than the stability the EU single currency was supposed to achieve.
The Maastricht treaty stipulates that countries joining EMU can have budget deficits no larger than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and overall debt levels not beyond 60 percent of GDP.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel has long insisted that EMU members must not let their deficits spill over the 3.0 percent line, but now finds himself so unexpectedly short of tax revenues that he cannot guarantee Germany will make the grade.
Waigel triggered off an unprecedented confrontation with the powerful Bundesbank when he suggested revaluing the central bank's gold stocks to fill his budget gaps.
The independent Bundesbank bluntly rejected the idea as interference in its business and an outright threat to the stability of the future euro currency.
